Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA View image in fullscreen Richard Tice is under investigation by parliament’s standards watchdog over a possible failure to declare an interest. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA Richard Tice Standards watchdog investigating Reform UK’s Richard Tice Party’s deputy leader says on social media the case is related to a complaint by an anti-Israel lobby group UK politics live – latest updates Aletha Adu Political correspondent Mon 3 Aug 2026 08.25 EDT First published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice , is under investigation by parliament’s standards watchdog over a possible failure to declare an interest. The watchdog did not provide details of the allegation aside from ⁠saying the case was opened on 28 July and would be conducted by the parliamentary commissioner for standards, Daniel ⁠Greenberg. As a matter of procedure, the watchdog never publicly releases details of an allegation being investigated until it has published its conclusion. Tice, the MP for Boston and Skegness, swiftly claimed on X that the inquiry related to a complaint over “whether I should have referenced my register of interests at the start of a debate on UK democracy and Israeli influence”. Without naming the group he was referring to, he wrote on X: “Contrary to garbage in media: Standards Commissioner is considering complaint by anti semitic anti Israel lobby group over whether I should have referenced my register of interests at start of a debate on UK democracy and Israeli influence.” A Labour party spokesperson said: “The Reform sleaze scandals continue to pile up. Richard Tice is now under investigation by the standards commissioner, on top of his firm avoiding paying £600,000 in tax. This means that both Reform’s leader and deputy leader now have standards investigations hanging over them. “With police probes, Nigel Farage’s secret £5m gift, and reports of funding from a convicted fraudster, it’s clear Reform think the rules just don’t apply to them.” Greenberg had also been investigating Farage, Reform UK’s leader, over a £5m gift he received in April 2024 from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian. That investigation was paused after Farage resigned as an MP last month and triggered a byelection for his Clacton seat in which he will stand again. The contest, in which all the other major political parties have refused to participate,, leaves Farage taking on 33 other candidates including Count Binface and Howling Laud Hope of the Official Monster Raving Looney party The Metropolitan police are also investigating payments to Reform UK, assessing payments made to the party via a company controlled by Tice. The police investigation came after the Guardian revealed last month that Fiona Cottrell made a £1m transfer to Britain Means Business, shortly before donations were made and about half of the funds were passed to Reform UK . Cottrell’s son George has close links to Farage. Last week, parliament’s standards watchdog declined to investigate a complaint made against Tice over an undeclared loan of £78,100 he received in December 2024, months after he was elected as the MP for Boston and Skegness. The commissioner told the Liberal Democrat MP Lisa Smart that he would not take further action on the basis that her complaint had not provided “sufficient evidence” to justify an investigation into a potential breach of conduct. Tice had said the loan was a corporate one, to one of his companies, which he said was not declarable. “I have a number of corporate loans in my companies. None of them are declarable. They are to do with my property business activities, not to do with politics,” Tice said, adding that his shareholdings and directorships were fully declared. In January last year, Tice gave £613,000 to Reform via Tisun Investments in an unusual case of an MP donating to their own party. A month later, a sum of £655,000 was paid into Tisun’s account in what was described by Tice as an overpayment for a property purchase. https://bnn-news.com/world/latvia-s-15th.text: Photo: BNN Advertisements At least 115,593 people, or 7.42% of Latvia’s 1,557,615 eligible voters, have cast their ballots so far ahead of the Saeima election, according to data compiled by the Central Election Commission (CVK). In Riga, at least 47,843 people, or 7.98% of eligible voters, have cast their ballots. This figure also includes 4,907 people abroad who registered to vote by post. For postal voting, the number of voters considered to have voted includes those who were sent voting materials and who have not voted or deposited a ballot for safekeeping in person at a polling station, the CVK explained. Among the regions, the highest turnout over the four days has been recorded in Vidzeme, where at least 33,134 voters, or 8.26%, have deposited their ballots for safekeeping. Advertisements In Zemgale, turnout has reached 6.53%, with 13,019 citizens having visited polling stations so far. In Kurzeme, at least 11,568 people, or 6.64%, have deposited their ballots, while in Latgale 10,029 voters have cast their ballots so far, representing 5.46% of eligible voters. As of Thursday, the highest turnout has been recorded in Ādaži Municipality, where 12.19% of registered eligible voters have cast their ballots. The lowest turnout has been recorded in Augšdaugava Municipality, at 4%. Data from some polling stations are still being awaited. Throughout the working days of this week, voters can deposit their ballots for safekeeping at any of the 933 polling stations across Latvia. The CVK explains that this form of voting is conceptually similar to advance voting, although there are some procedural differences that allow voters to change their minds during the week leading up to election day and replace the ballot they have already deposited. Advertisements The official Saeima election day is Saturday. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3ew.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The St Petersburg Oil Terminal was among targets hit in the city overnight By Aleks Phillips Published 3 hours ago At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities. The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five. A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit. Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week. Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing. It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel. Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July . Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday. St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed. He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible. Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning. Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire. It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes". As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions. Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections. Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort. Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism , including from some US Republicans. Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year. Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years. Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter. Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.
